fixes.explanation: Right, friend. The LORD says, “And I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria.” (Isaiah 38:6) That's a promise about the king's life and about his whole city. The LORD adds, “I will defend this city.” (Isaiah 38:6)

That's right, baker. The text says Hezekiah had asked, “What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?” (Isaiah 38:22) I think a man who had been that sick would be eager to go up to the house of the LORD.
This one is True, friend. The text says Hezekiah had asked, “What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?” (Isaiah 38:22) He did ask, and it's right there in the last verse.

I get why you'd think that, baker, because most of us hope the news will be good. But Isaiah, the prophet, brings the opposite. The LORD's word is, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” (Isaiah 38:1) I think this one is a heavy moment.

That's right, friend. The message says the king will NOT recover. Isaiah, the prophet, tells him, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” (Isaiah 38:1) I think this one hurts.
Gold is a fair guess, but it never comes up in his prayer. He asks the LORD to remember how he has walked “…faithfully and with wholehearted devotion…” (Isaiah 38:3) No receipts, no donation totals.
That's right, baker. The LORD tells Isaiah to say He is “…the God of your father David…” (Isaiah 38:5) So the message comes from the LORD, and He names David right there.
I see why Babylon came to mind, baker. But the LORD names someone else here. “…I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria.” (Isaiah 38:6) Stick with Assyria for this one.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, “I will make the sun’s shadow that falls on the stairway of Ahaz go back ten steps.” (Isaiah 38:8) And then the text tells us, “So the sunlight went back the ten steps it had descended.” I've watched a lot of timers tick down, and I have NEVER seen one go back ten.

A king missing his throne makes sense, friend. But that's not what he says. He says, “I will never again see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living…” (Isaiah 38:11) I think what he's afraid of losing is far bigger than a chair.
A vine is a good guess, since cutting one off is easy to picture. But a weaver works at a loom, and the text says, “He cuts me off from the loom…” (Isaiah 38:12) Think threads, not vines.
Right, baker. Hezekiah prays, “O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.” (Isaiah 38:14) He's weak and worn out, and he asks the Lord to stand behind him.
This one is True, friend. Hezekiah says, “I will walk slowly all my years because of the anguish of my soul.” (Isaiah 38:15) Those are his own words, and I think the hard season stays with him.
That's it, baker. Hezekiah says, “The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today…” (Isaiah 38:19) He says "the living" twice, and I bet he's still amazed he's one of them.
That's a reasonable word, but it isn't the one Hezekiah uses. He says, “fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness.” (Isaiah 38:19) Faithfulness is the word the verse gives.
Yes, baker. The text says, “Prepare a lump of pressed figs and apply it to the boil, and he will recover.” (Isaiah 38:21) That's Isaiah's exact instruction.
